misconceptions.statement: A median is the line from a vertex that cuts the opposite side at a right angle.
misconceptions.why: Students mix up the median with the altitude because both start at a vertex and end on the opposite side.
misconceptions.fix: A median goes to the midpoint of the opposite side, so it splits that side into two equal parts. It need not be perpendicular to the side.

probe.question: In triangle ABC, D is the midpoint of BC. Is AD a median only if AD is perpendicular to BC?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, a median must meet the side at 90 degrees.

misconceptions.root_belief: similar-sounding terms mean the same thing
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of student errors in geometry vocabulary and concept definitions

misconceptions.statement: A median can lie outside the triangle.
misconceptions.why: Students carry over what they saw for altitudes of obtuse triangles.
misconceptions.fix: All three medians always lie inside the triangle and meet at one point, the centroid.

probe.question: Can the median of an obtuse triangle fall outside the triangle?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it can fall outside like the altitude does.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule for one case applies to all similar cases

misconceptions.statement: An altitude must bisect the side it falls on.
misconceptions.why: Students see altitudes drawn in isosceles or equilateral triangles where it also is a median.
misconceptions.fix: An altitude only needs to be perpendicular to the opposite side. It splits the side into equal parts only in special triangles like isosceles or equilateral.

probe.question: In a scalene triangle, does the altitude from a vertex always meet the opposite side at its midpoint?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the altitude always cuts the side in half.

misconceptions.root_belief: features of a special example hold for all cases
misconceptions.source_hint: research on prototype images in geometry concept formation

misconceptions.statement: The altitude is the slanted side of the triangle, not a separate line.
misconceptions.why: The everyday word height and the word side get mixed; students read the slant side as the height.
misconceptions.fix: The altitude is a new line drawn from a vertex perpendicular to the opposite side. It is usually not one of the sides.

probe.question: In a triangle with sides 5, 6, 7 cm, what is the altitude to the 6 cm base?
probe.wrong_answer: 5 cm or 7 cm, the slanting side.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student difficulties with height of triangles

misconceptions.statement: An altitude always lies inside the triangle.
misconceptions.why: Textbook diagrams mostly show acute triangles with the base horizontal.
misconceptions.fix: In an obtuse triangle two altitudes lie outside it, and in a right triangle two altitudes are the legs themselves.

probe.question: In an obtuse triangle, where do the altitudes from the two acute vertices lie?
probe.wrong_answer: Inside the triangle.

misconceptions.root_belief: the usual picture shows every possible case
misconceptions.source_hint: research on prototypical diagrams and orientation in geometry

misconceptions.statement: The angle sum of a triangle depends on how big the triangle is.
misconceptions.why: Students think bigger shapes have bigger angle totals since the sides are longer.
misconceptions.fix: Every triangle, big or small, has angles that add to exactly 180 degrees.

probe.question: Is the angle sum of a large triangle more than that of a small triangle?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the larger triangle has a bigger angle sum.

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect
misconceptions.source_hint: studies on angle as size of side length misconceptions

misconceptions.statement: The angle sum is 180 degrees only for some triangles like equilateral or right-angled ones.
misconceptions.why: Students learn the rule via a few special triangles and assume it is limited to them.
misconceptions.fix: The angle sum is 180 degrees for every kind of triangle, including scalene and obtuse ones.

probe.question: What is the sum of angles of an obtuse scalene triangle?
probe.wrong_answer: More than 180 degrees, since one angle is large.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule works only for the examples shown

misconceptions.statement: A triangle can have two right angles or two obtuse angles.
misconceptions.why: Students do not link the 180-degree total to what angles are possible together.
misconceptions.fix: Because the three angles add to 180 degrees, a triangle can have at most one right or obtuse angle.

probe.question: Can a triangle have angles 90, 90 and 0? Or 100, 100 and a small angle?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, 100, 100 and 10 is possible.

misconceptions.root_belief: facts are separate and do not constrain each other

misconceptions.statement: To find the missing angle, subtract the given angle from 180 and stop.
misconceptions.why: Students use a one-step subtraction without noting there are two other angles.
misconceptions.fix: Subtract the sum of both known angles from 180. If only one angle is known, you need more information.

probe.question: Two angles of a triangle are 50 and 60 degrees. Find the third.
probe.wrong_answer: 130 degrees (180 minus 50).

misconceptions.root_belief: a familiar procedure fits any similar problem

misconceptions.statement: An exterior angle is any angle outside the triangle, drawn anywhere.
misconceptions.why: Students read exterior as simply outside the figure.
misconceptions.fix: An exterior angle is formed at a vertex when one side is extended, and it makes a linear pair with the interior angle at that vertex.

probe.question: Which angle is exterior at vertex C when side BC is extended to D?
probe.wrong_answer: The angle on the other side of the triangle, not touching the extended line.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: The exterior angle equals the sum of all three interior angles.
misconceptions.why: Students recall that interior angles add to 180 and merge the two rules.
misconceptions.fix: The exterior angle equals the sum of only the two interior opposite angles, not the adjacent one.

probe.question: Interior angles are 40, 60, 80. What is the exterior angle at the 80 degree vertex?
probe.wrong_answer: 180 degrees.

misconceptions.root_belief: two related rules are really the same rule
misconceptions.source_hint: classroom error analyses of angle property application in geometry

misconceptions.statement: The exterior angle equals the adjacent interior angle.
misconceptions.why: Students see both angles at the same vertex and think they match.
misconceptions.fix: The exterior angle and the adjacent interior angle add to 180 degrees; they are a linear pair.

probe.question: Interior angle at C is 70 degrees. What is the exterior angle at C?
probe.wrong_answer: 70 degrees.

misconceptions.root_belief: nearby things must be equal

misconceptions.statement: The exterior angle is always obtuse.
misconceptions.why: Students mostly see diagrams with an acute or right triangle angle giving a large exterior angle.
misconceptions.fix: The exterior angle is obtuse only if the adjacent interior angle is acute; if the interior angle is obtuse, the exterior angle is acute.

probe.question: A triangle has an interior angle of 120 degrees. Is the exterior angle at that vertex obtuse?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, exterior angles are always obtuse.

misconceptions.root_belief: the typical picture is always true

misconceptions.statement: If the sum of two sides is equal to the third, a triangle can still be formed.
misconceptions.why: Students think equal is enough since the lengths seem to touch.
misconceptions.fix: The sum of any two sides must be strictly greater than the third. If equal, the sides lie flat along a line.

probe.question: Can a triangle have sides 3 cm, 4 cm and 7 cm?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because 3 + 4 equals 7.

misconceptions.root_belief: borderline cases count as inside the rule
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student reasoning about triangle existence conditions

misconceptions.statement: Any three lengths can form a triangle.
misconceptions.why: Students think of drawing any three segments and joining them.
misconceptions.fix: Three lengths form a triangle only if each pair adds to more than the third length.

probe.question: Can sides 2 cm, 3 cm and 8 cm form a triangle?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, any three lengths can.

misconceptions.root_belief: anything can be built if we have the parts
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of triangle construction and existence tasks

misconceptions.statement: It is enough to check that the two smaller sides add to more than the largest; no other checks are needed — wait, checking only the two shortest is not enough.
misconceptions.why: Students pick pairs at random and check one only.
misconceptions.fix: Checking the two shortest sides against the longest is enough, but checking two other sides (like the longest two against the shortest) proves nothing about the triangle.

probe.question: For 3, 4, 8 cm, a student checks 4 + 8 > 3 and decides a triangle exists. Is that right?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, since one pair satisfied the rule.

misconceptions.root_belief: one check proves the whole rule

misconceptions.statement: The difference of two sides can be equal to or more than the third side.
misconceptions.why: Students remember only the sum rule and ignore the difference rule.
misconceptions.fix: The difference of any two sides is less than the third side.

probe.question: Sides 3 cm and 10 cm: can the third side be 6 cm?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because 10 minus 3 is 7, which is more than 6.

misconceptions.root_belief: remember only half of a two-part rule

misconceptions.statement: The hypotenuse is the bottom side of a right triangle, the one drawn horizontally.
misconceptions.why: Textbook diagrams usually show the hypotenuse as the slanted side, but other orientations confuse students into labelling the base.
misconceptions.fix: The hypotenuse is always the side opposite the right angle, whichever way the triangle is turned.

probe.question: A right triangle has its right angle at the top and a horizontal bottom side. Which side is the hypotenuse?
probe.wrong_answer: One of the slanting sides.

misconceptions.root_belief: orientation in the picture defines the thing
misconceptions.source_hint: research on orientation of figures in geometry misconceptions

misconceptions.statement: In a right triangle, hypotenuse = a + b.
misconceptions.why: Students treat squares as unnecessary and add the lengths instead of squares.
misconceptions.fix: The squares are added: a² + b² = c². The sides themselves do not add to the hypotenuse.

probe.question: Legs are 3 and 4 cm. Find the hypotenuse.
probe.wrong_answer: 7 cm.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from whole numbers works everywhere
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student errors with the Pythagorean theorem

misconceptions.statement: Pythagoras property holds for every triangle.
misconceptions.why: Students remember the formula but not that it needs a right angle.
misconceptions.fix: It applies only to right-angled triangles.

probe.question: Triangle has sides 4, 5 and 6 cm. Is 4² + 5² = 6²?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it holds for all triangles.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule works everywhere once learned
misconceptions.source_hint: research on application of Pythagorean theorem to non-right triangles

misconceptions.statement: To find a leg, add the squares of the hypotenuse and the other leg.
misconceptions.why: Students apply the formula 'add squares' mechanically even when the unknown is a leg.
misconceptions.fix: If the hypotenuse is known, subtract: leg² = hypotenuse² − other leg².

probe.question: Hypotenuse is 13 cm and one leg is 5 cm. Find the other leg.

misconceptions.root_belief: one fixed procedure applies to all versions
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student errors in finding unknown sides with Pythagoras

misconceptions.statement: After finding c², the answer is c² itself, no square root is needed.
misconceptions.why: Students stop at the squared value and forget the last step.
misconceptions.fix: c² is the square of the length; take the square root to get the side length.

probe.question: Legs are 6 and 8 cm. What is the hypotenuse?

misconceptions.root_belief: stopping a procedure one step early still finishes it
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student errors in Pythagoras calculations

misconceptions.statement: If a² + b² = c² for three sides, the triangle may still not be right-angled.
misconceptions.why: Students see the converse as unproven or separate from the property.
misconceptions.fix: If the squares of two sides add up to the square of the third, the triangle is right-angled, with the right angle opposite the third side.

probe.question: Is a triangle with sides 5, 12, 13 cm right-angled?
probe.wrong_answer: Not necessarily, we need to measure the angles.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule does not work in reverse

misconceptions.statement: When checking for a right triangle, the largest side should be treated as one of the legs.
misconceptions.why: Students add the squares of any two sides without taking the longest as c.
misconceptions.fix: The longest side must be the one that is tested as the hypotenuse: check if the other two squares add up to its square.

probe.question: Sides 5, 12, 13: is 5² + 13² = 12²?
probe.wrong_answer: No, so it is not right-angled.

misconceptions.root_belief: order of items in a rule does not matter
